newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Shortened trading, lot of data.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Shortened trading, lot of data.

text.p: So much data, so little time; that's what the U.S. credit markets face this coming week with one trading session cancelled and two sessions shortened for Thursday's Thanksgiving Day holiday.

After appetizers like the October existing home sales report Monday and weekly store sales and the Conference Board's November consumer confidence figures Tuesday, the market gets a data cornucopia Wednesday befitting a pre-Thanksgiving Day feast.

Third-quarter GDP was first reported to be 2.2 percent but a sizable drop in September wholesale inventories led economists polled by Reuters to conclude, on average, that the 2.2 percent figure will be revised downward to 1.7 percent.
Jobless claims data for the week ended Nov 16 will also be served up at 0830 EST Wednesday.
"Jobless claims will let us see whether this week's spike (up to 344,000 new claims) was a fluke or not," said Marrone.
"Jobless claims have been the one item challenging the notion that we're in a broad-based slowdown," said James Glassman, vice president and economist at Chase Securities.
October durable goods orders, rescheduled for release Wednesday at 1000 EST, is like a recipe whose outcome is always in doubt.

"Durable goods is so volatile," said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market analyst at UBS Securities. "There are so many categories (of orders) that there's usually something in it for everybody."

Economists Reuters polled estimated, on average, that durable goods fell 2.0 percent in October after jumping 4.9 percent in September. Without defense orders, they forecast a 2.2 percent orders drop after a 4.8 percent September rise.
Yet Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co, said durable goods is one of the two meatiest reports the market will get in the coming week.
"The market often looks to the durable goods data for some leading information on the manufacturing sector," he said.

The same is true of the November Chicago Purchasing Managers report, also due at 1000 EST, which the market will savor, trying to sift out some foretaste of the November National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) report due the Monday after the Thanksiving closure.

"The Chicago Purchasing Managers index is a good read on manufacturing conditions in the middle of the country and though there's no direct corelation to the NAPM, people do draw inferences," said Youngdahl.
A little input from the consumer sector is also on tap for 1000 EST Wednesday from the University of Michigan's final November measure of consumer sentiment.

"If high consumer confidence translates into strong retail sales at Christmas, that could be a damper on our expectations for lower interest rates," observed Greg Carr, market analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.

Youngdahl said the only chance for a major market in the Thanksgiving week would come from "some change in perception (about the economy's direction) based either on the durable goods data or on the Chicago PMI." If weekly jobless claims were to stay near 340,000, that, too, could be viewed as more evidence of a slowing economy, he said.
Trading will end three hours early Wednesday before the Thursday Thanksgiving holiday and will resume on Friday for another shortened session.
The October personal income and consumption data, due Friday, will be viewed as slightly stale, analysts said, and thus unlikely to excite the market's palate.
Conference Board's October Help-Wanted Advertising index and some Federal Reserve's money and banking figures are also certain to be market non-events.

Trading desks will operate with skeletal staffs on Friday during a shortened trading session that will likely prove to be no more than a mildly inconvenient interruption of a long Thanksgiving Day holiday weekend.
Dealers indicated Fed funds would open between 5-1/4 and 5-5/8 percent Monday.
The 6benchmark -1/2 percent 30-year Treasury bond was down 9/32 at 100-25/32 to yield 6.44 percent in late Friday trade.
